work.title: Passion of Terentius, Africanus, Pompeius and their companions (20 March)

paragraphs.text: March 20. The martyrdom of Saints Terentius, Africanus, and Pompeius. While Decius was reigning over the Roman dominion and wishing to draw everyone to his own faith—for he had the devil as his father— he sent orders throughout his empire that all who called upon the name of Christ should be induced to eat defiled food. If any resisted this, they were to be handed over for judgment. He also sent this impious command to Africa, to Fortunatianus, the governor of Africa. When the emperor's command reached his jurisdiction, the governor received the emperor's letter and sat on the judgment seat. He ordered the townspeople to be seized and brought in, and instruments of torture to be laid before them.

He said to them: “Sacrifice to the gods. Otherwise, you will die a terrible death.” Many of the people, seeing the instruments of torture and fearing the threats, obeyed the governor and abandoned the faith of Christ. But some of them, forty in number, pledged to meet their end [?], gathering together. And they said with confidence to one another: “Take care, brothers. Let us not deny our Lord Jesus Christ, so that he in turn will not deny us. Understand that the Lord has already said: ‘Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul. Rather, fear the one who can destroy both soul and body in the fiery [?].’” They strengthened one another with these words. Fortunatianus the governor said: “I see that you are men of fine stature, handsome and wise in speech. How have you given yourselves over to such deception, deception, confessing one God and a certain Christ, whom Jewish youths crucified as a criminal?” The holy martyr Terentius, speaking for them all, said:

“If the governor knew the power of the crucified one, he would abandon the vain deception of idols and worship him and please him, the true Son, the benefactor from the Father, compassionate and merciful, who at the Father's bidding and command came down to earth and adorned his divinity with human nature, and who also endured the cross for our salvation.” When Fortunatianus the governor heard this, he said to the saints: “Will you sacrifice, or shall I lay hands on your limbs and destroy you?” Terentius said: “Did you think we would be frightened by threats? We are not so weak that we would abandon the giver of life and worship foreign gods. Just do whatever you wish to us.” Then the governor became angry. He ordered their clothes to be torn off and the prisoners to be led into the temple of the idols. These shrines were gilded and adorned with costly splendor. The governor entered and said to them, “Offer sacrifice to the great-minded god Heracles. You see his glory and his power.” Terentius said, “You are deceiving yourself, not knowing what is good for you.

For these whom you regard as gods are stone, wood, bronze, and iron, adorned with gold to lead people astray from eternal life. For they neither see nor speak nor walk nor hear, being stones, carved by human beings and fashioned in human form. So speak to your gods, as you consider them, and see whether they can help themselves or inflict [?] on anyone who is angry with them.” Hearing this, the governor became furious and ordered Terentius and Africanus, Maximus and Pompeius, to be thrown into the inner prison and kept under the strictest guard, saying, “I will question them on [?] day.” But blessed Zeno, Alexander, and Theodore, together with their companions, forty-six in number, he ordered to be brought before the judgment seat. He said to them, “You have gained nothing by your earlier argument. Listen to me and offer sacrifice to great-minded Heracles.” They answered, “We have told you many times, including at your first interrogation, that we are Christians, and you will not persuade us to worship at unclean shrines. For we are ready, when you question us,

to answer.” The governor said, “Will you not listen to me when I appeal to you? Then you are forcing me to carry out the emperor’s command and inflict further things on you.” He ordered them to be beaten with knotted rods and ox sinews. The holy martyrs stretched out their hands toward heaven and cried out in a loud voice, “Look upon us, O God, and help your servants, and deliver us from the adversary!” Hearing this, the governor ordered them to be beaten still more severely, until thirty centurions had taken turns beating each of them. As the saints were being beaten, the [?] and the rods wore out. Then, in a fury, he ordered them to be beaten with knotty pieces of wood, so that even their internal organs could now be seen. This was what the saints looked like, so that everyone marveled at their endurance. After they had been tortured severely, the governor said, “At least offer sacrifice now, you wretches, and I will release you.” But the saints remained silent, giving him no answer. Again the governor ordered nails to be heated and their backs burned with them. And when they were torturing them severely, he ordered strong vinegar mixed with salt

to be poured onto their backs, and their wounds to be rubbed with coarse cloth. The saints looked up to heaven: “Lord God, who delivered your three holy youths, Hananiah, Azariah, and Mishael, from the fiery furnace and did not allow them to suffer harm; who delivered Daniel from the lions’ mouths and preserved Moses from Pharaoh’s hand; who saved Thecla from the fire, from the arena, and from the beasts; who work and bestow banners on those you love; who raised up the shepherd of the sheep, our Lord Jesus Christ; who have bestowed many and varied blessings; who have made light shine and have driven darkness away; who roll up heaven like a hide; who count the stars of heaven and the sand of the sea, and have adorned truth: hear us as we pray to you, O Christ, and help us, for yours are the glory and the power forever. Amen.” When the saints had finished their prayer and said “Amen,” the governor again ordered them to be hung up and their sides scraped. As the saints were being flayed for many hours, a stream of blood flowed from their holy bodies, so that the great quantity of blood

soaked the attendants’ clothes. Yet they paid no heed to the tortures, for Christ was giving them relief and helping them. The governor said to them, “Have the tortures persuaded you to give up the madness you possess, you who are doomed to a miserable death, or do you persist in your false belief?” But the saints gave him no answer. Instead, they looked up to heaven and said, “You who demolished the city of Sodom with fire and laid it waste, send your help now as well, and destroy this godless madness and overthrow their idols.” Then, making the sign of the cross on their faces, they blew upon the idols, and immediately they crumbled and became like dust. The saints said to the lawless governor, “Look at the things you worship! Where is their empty strength? Were they able to help themselves?” While the saints were saying this, the temple of the idols also collapsed. The governor became enraged at the destruction of his gods. He ordered the saints to be put to death by the sword. When the saints received the sentence, they went away rejoicing and praising the Lord. When they reached the appointed place, they knelt down and stretched out

their necks, and died by the sword, confessing Christ. Christians came, took their bodies, and laid them in a place of honor. After these saints had died, the lawless governor ordered Terentius and Africanus to be brought in. He said to them, “Offer sacrifices to the gods. Otherwise, I will put you both to a cruel death, and there is no god who will deliver you from my hands.” The two saints replied, “We have told you many times that we are Christians and place our hope in Christ. We will not bow down to unclean demons or serve your gods, and we care nothing for your tortures. So devise as many tortures against us as you wish. For we trust in God that you will be defeated by us, his servants, just as your father the devil was defeated.” When the governor heard this, he ordered them to be thrown into prison and chains to be placed around their necks, on their hands, and on their feet, and for them to be kept under guard in this condition. The servants did as they had been commanded. He also ordered iron tridents to be laid beneath them, and that no Christian should be allowed to visit them or give them food.

At midnight, while the two saints were praying, a great light shone around them in the prison. An angel of the Lord stood before them and said, “Rise and rest.” The angel approached and touched the chains that lay around their necks, and immediately the chains fell from their bodies. Before them stood a table prepared with all kinds of good food. The angel said to them, “Take some of the food set before you, which the Lord God has sent you.” The two saints blessed the Lord and then ate the food. When the prison guards saw the light, they rushed inside to see the light more clearly. When they entered, they found the two saints rejoicing, and they went out in fear. They reported to the governor what they had seen. On the third day, he ordered the saints to be brought before the judgment seat. When the two saints stood before the governor, he said to them, “Have the tortures taught you your lesson, then?” “O you wicked, demon-possessed ones! Repent and sacrifice to the gods.” Saint Terence said, “This torture, for me

and for those who love Christ, may it be! For the foolishness of God is wiser than human beings. For human wisdom is foolishness before God. I would be senseless and raving, like you, if I abandoned God and worshiped demons.” The governor became angry and ordered them to be flayed. As the two saints were being scraped, they prayed, saying, “Jesus Christ, Son of the living God, light of Christians who abides forever, indestructible faith, appear and help us both, and do not put us to shame before your face.” While the servants were flaying them and Christ was easing their torments, the two saints felt no pain. The governor became angry and ordered them to be taken down from the wooden frame and led into prison. He summoned all the beast-charmers and ordered them to bring as many creatures as they had, fierce and vicious ones—asps, vipers, and horned snakes—and to throw them in and shut them up with the two saints. The creatures crawled about before their feet as they sat, and did not touch them at all. The two saints sang and praised God. The creatures remained shut up with them for three days and three nights. On the fourth day, the governor sent men at night

to see whether the two saints had been killed by the creatures. Those who had been sent came to the prison doors to listen. They heard them singing and praising God. Wishing to see more clearly, they climbed onto the prison building and looked down through the small doors. They saw the two saints sitting and an angel of the Lord standing before the creatures, not allowing them to come near. They ran and reported to the governor what they had seen. The governor rose early in the morning, sat on the judgment seat, and ordered the charmers to take the creatures away and to bring the two saints before the judgment seat. The charmers went and, wishing to approach the doors so that the creatures would come to them, called them with their spells, but the creatures did not obey them. When they opened the prison doors, all the creatures came out together and killed all the people they found standing there. Then they went away into deserted places. The prison guards went, took the two saints, and led them to the governor. When the tormentor saw that the two saints had suffered no harm at all, he flew into a rage

He gave his verdict concerning them: to put them to death with the sword. The two saints went away rejoicing, singing and saying: “He saved us from those who afflicted us and prevailed over those who hated us.” The soldiers appointed to this task took up the sword and cut off the heads of the two saints. And they died confessing Christ. Christian men came and took the bodies of the two saints, carefully prepared them for burial, and laid them in a place of honor, two miles away from the city of Rome. The saints suffered martyrdom— Terentius and Africanus, Maximus and Pompey, and their companions—under the emperor and persecutor Decius and Valerian, while our Lord Jesus Christ reigns over us. To him be glory and dominion forever and ever. Amen.
